newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia, UN yet to name date for Slavonia polls.
newsitem.headline: Croatia, UN yet to name date for Slavonia polls.

text.p: Local elections in the Serb-run region of Eastern Slavonia will be held together with those in the rest of the country, but the exact date remains to be set by the government, officials said on Monday.

"(Eastern Slavonia) is part of Croatia and the goal is to have elections at the same time to symbolise that this really is one entity, that message is very important," said Jacques Klein, the U.N. administrator of the region.
The U.S. diplomat, who heads the U.N. Transitional Administration of Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), spoke to reporters after meeting Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and his cabinet in Zagreb on Monday.

The talks were expected to produce an official announcement about the date of the local and municipal elections, to be held simultaneously in Eastern Slavonia and elsewhere in Croatia, which were put earlier by various sources, including the U.N. and the Croatian government, at March 16.

"I discussed with the president the dates. He obviously wants now to consult with his ministers and then we will try to find a date that meets the needs of everyone, that allows enough time to have a fair election," Klein said.
"The president has to decide. That's his call," he added.
Ivica Kostovic, a government minister in charge of peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, said Zagreb will make a final decision in the next two days.
"The Croatian government will determine today and tomorrow the date of the elections in Croatia, and the UNTAES will then conform with the decision," Kostovic said.

The Croatian daily Vjesnik speculated over the weekend that the elections could be postponed for a week or two, but Kostovic and Klein both insisted there could be no talk of postponment when the exact date has never been set officially.
Minority Serbs, who took control over the region during Croatian bid to secede from former Yugoslavia in 1991, took to the streets over the weekend to demand changes in Croatian legislation.
Serbs want the region, now split in two administrative units or "zupanije", unified into one, a demand that Croatian government dismissed outright.

A series of shooting incidents, including a killing of a Belgian U.N. soldier ten days ago, have increased tensions in an area that is supposed to come under complete Croatian control after U.N. troops pull out on July 15.
Klein blamed a small group of extremists among the Serb leadership for stalling the progress towards unification.
"We are not going to let few people who are trying to undermine the process of peaceful reintegration to stand in our way. That I will not tolerate," Klein said.
The appointed mayor of Vukovar Miroslav Keravica was among those who told his people not to apply for Croatian documents, necessary for taking part in the elections.
